# SchemaWrite in wincode - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wincode/^0.5.0/trait.SchemaWrite.html

`pub unsafe trait SchemaWrite<C: `[ConfigCore](https://docs.rs/config/trait.ConfigCore.html)> {
    type [Src](https://docs.rs#associatedtype.Src): ?[Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sized.html);
    const [TYPE_META](https://docs.rs#associatedconstant.TYPE_META): [TypeMeta](https://docs.rs/enum.TypeMeta.html) = TypeMeta::Dynamic;
    // Required methods
    fn [size_of](https://docs.rs#tymethod.size_of)(src: &Self::[Src](https://docs.rs/trait.SchemaWrite.html#associatedtype.Src)) -> [WriteResult](https://docs.rs/error/type.WriteResult.html)<[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)>;
[write](https://docs.rs#tymethod.write)(writer: impl [Writer](https://docs.rs/io/trait.Writer.html), src: &Self::[Src](https://docs.rs/trait.SchemaWrite.html#associatedtype.Src)) -> [WriteResult](https://docs.rs/error/type.WriteResult.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html)>;
}## Expand description

## Provided Associated Constants[§](https://docs.rs#provided-associated-consts)

Metadata about the type’s serialization.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety-1)Safety

It is always safe to leave this as the default `TypeMeta::Dynamic`. If
you set it to `TypeMeta::Static { size, zero_copy }`, you have to ensure
the following two points:

- `size`must always correspond to the number of bytes written by- `write`.- `size_of`must always return- `Ok(size)`.
- If `zero_copy`is`true`,`Src`’s in-memory representation must correspond exactly to the serialized form. There must be no padding in the in-memory representation of`Src`.

## Required Associated Types[§](https://docs.rs#required-associated-types)

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

    type [Dst](https://docs.rs#associatedtype.Dst);

}## Expand description

## Provided Associated Constants[§](https://docs.rs#provided-associated-consts)

Metadata about the type’s serialization.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety-1)Safety

It is always safe to leave this as the default `TypeMeta::Dynamic`. If
you set it to `TypeMeta::Static { size, zero_copy }`, you have to ensure
the following two points:

- `size`must always correspond to the number of bytes read by- `read`.
- If `zero_copy`is`true`,`Dst`’s in-memory representation must correspond exactly to the serialized form, and all byte sequences must be valid in-memory representations of`Dst`.

## Required Associated Types[§](https://docs.rs#required-associated-types)

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/wincode/schema/mod.rs.html#283)#### fn [read](https://docs.rs#tymethod.read)(
    reader: impl [Reader](https://docs.rs/io/trait.Reader.html)<'de>,
    dst: &mut [MaybeUninit](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/mem/maybe_uninit/union.MaybeUninit.html)<Self::[Dst](https://docs.rs/trait.SchemaRead.html#associatedtype.Dst)>,
) -> [ReadResult](https://docs.rs/error/type.ReadResult.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/wincode/schema/mod.rs.html#283)

#### fn [read](https://docs.rs#tymethod.read)(
    reader: impl [Reader](https://docs.rs/io/trait.Reader.html)<'de>,
    dst: &mut [MaybeUninit](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/mem/maybe_uninit/union.MaybeUninit.html)<Self::[Dst](https://docs.rs/trait.SchemaRead.html#associatedtype.Dst)>,
) -> [ReadResult](https://docs.rs/error/type.ReadResult.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html)>

Read into `dst` from `reader`.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety-2)Safety

You must initialize `dst` if **and only if** you return `Ok(())`. In the
`Err(…)` case, initializing `dst` can lead to memory leaks.

It is permissible to not initialize `dst` if `dst` is an inhabited
zero-sized type.

## Provided Methods[§](https://docs.rs#provided-methods)

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

# deserialize_mut in wincode - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wincode/^0.5.0/fn.deserialize_mut.html

`pub fn deserialize_mut<'de, T>(src: &'de mut [`[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)]) -> [ReadResult](https://docs.rs/error/type.ReadResult.html)<T>## Expand description

Deserialize a type from the given bytes, with the ability
to form mutable references for types that are [ ZeroCopy](https://docs.rs/trait.ZeroCopy.html).
This can allow mutating the serialized data in place.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

[§](https://docs.rs#zero-copy-types)Zero-copy types

```
#[derive(SchemaWrite, SchemaRead)]
#[repr(C)]
struct Data {
    bytes: [u8; 7],
    the_answer: u8,
}
let data = Data { bytes: [0; 7], the_answer: 0 };
let mut serialized = wincode::serialize(&data).unwrap();
let data_mut: &mut Data = wincode::deserialize_mut(&mut serialized).unwrap();
data_mut.bytes = *b"wincode";
data_mut.the_answer = 42;
let deserialized: Data = wincode::deserialize(&serialized).unwrap();
assert_eq!(deserialized, Data { bytes: *b"wincode", the_answer: 42 });
```
[§](https://docs.rs#mutable-zero-copy-members)Mutable zero-copy members

```
#[derive(SchemaWrite, SchemaRead)]
struct Data {
    bytes: [u8; 7],
    the_answer: u8,
}
#[derive(SchemaRead)]
struct DataMut<'a> {
    bytes: &'a mut [u8; 7],
    the_answer: u8,
}
let data = Data { bytes: [0; 7], the_answer: 42 };
let mut serialized = wincode::serialize(&data).unwrap();
let data_mut: DataMut<'_> = wincode::deserialize_mut(&mut serialized).unwrap();
*data_mut.bytes = *b"wincode";
let deserialized: Data = wincode::deserialize(&serialized).unwrap();
assert_eq!(deserialized, Data { bytes: *b"wincode", the_answer: 42 });
```

---

# ZeroCopy in wincode - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wincode/^0.5.0/trait.ZeroCopy.html

`pub unsafe trait ZeroCopy: `[ZeroCopy](https://docs.rs/config/trait.ZeroCopy.html)<[DefaultConfig](https://docs.rs/config/type.DefaultConfig.html)> {
    // Provided methods
    fn [from_bytes](https://docs.rs#method.from_bytes)<'de>(bytes: &'de [[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)]) -> [ReadResult](https://docs.rs/error/type.ReadResult.html)<&'de Self>
       where Self: [SchemaRead](https://docs.rs/trait.SchemaRead.html)<'de, [DefaultConfig](https://docs.rs/config/type.DefaultConfig.html), Dst = Self> + [Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sized.html) { ... }
[from_bytes_mut](https://docs.rs#method.from_bytes_mut)<'de>(bytes: &'de mut [[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)]) -> [ReadResult](https://docs.rs/error/type.ReadResult.html)<&'de mut Self>
       where Self: [SchemaRead](https://docs.rs/trait.SchemaRead.html)<'de, [DefaultConfig](https://docs.rs/config/type.DefaultConfig.html), Dst = Self> + [Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sized.html) { ... }
}## Expand description

Marker trait for types that can be deserialized via direct borrows from a [ Reader](https://docs.rs/io/trait.Reader.html)
using the default configuration. See

[for configuration aware methods.](https://docs.rs/config/trait.ZeroCopy.html)

`config::ZeroCopy`Always prefer using [ config::ZeroCopy](https://docs.rs/config/trait.ZeroCopy.html) for your implementations to keep them fully
generic.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

- The type must not have any invalid bit patterns, no layout requirements, no endianness checks, etc.

## Provided Methods[§](https://docs.rs#provided-methods)

Get a reference to a type from the given bytes.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
#[derive(SchemaWrite, SchemaRead)]
#[repr(C)]
struct Data {
    bytes: [u8; 7],
    the_answer: u8,
}
let data = Data { bytes: *b"wincode", the_answer: 42 };

```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/wincode/schema/mod.rs.html#409-414)#### fn [from_bytes_mut](https://docs.rs#method.from_bytes_mut)<'de>(bytes: &'de mut [[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)]) -> [ReadResult](https://docs.rs/error/type.ReadResult.html)<&'de mut Self>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/wincode/schema/mod.rs.html#409-414)

#### fn [from_bytes_mut](https://docs.rs#method.from_bytes_mut)<'de>(bytes: &'de mut [[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)]) -> [ReadResult](https://docs.rs/error/type.ReadResult.html)<&'de mut Self>

Get a mutable reference to a type from the given bytes.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-1)Examples

```
#[derive(SchemaWrite, SchemaRead)]
#[repr(C)]
struct Data {
    bytes: [u8; 7],
    the_answer: u8,
}
let data = Data { bytes: [0; 7], the_answer: 0 };
let mut serialized = wincode::serialize(&data).unwrap();
let data_mut = Data::from_bytes_mut(&mut serialized).unwrap();
data_mut.bytes = *b"wincode";
data_mut.the_answer = 42;
let deserialized: Data = wincode::deserialize(&serialized).unwrap();
assert_eq!(deserialized, Data { bytes: *b"wincode", the_answer: 42 });
```

# pod_wrapper in wincode - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wincode/^0.5.0/macro.pod_wrapper.html

```
macro_rules! pod_wrapper {
    ($(unsafe struct $name:ident($type:ty);)*) => { ... };
}
```
## Expand description

Creates a wrapper type for a type that is represented by raw bytes and does not have any invalid bit patterns.

By using `pod_wrapper!`, you are telling wincode that it can serialize and deserialize a type
with a single memcpy – it wont pay attention to things like struct layout, endianness, or
anything else that would require validity or bit pattern checks. This is a very strong claim to
make, so be sure that your type adheres to those requirements.

Composable with sequence [ containers](https://docs.rs/containers/index.html) or compound types (structs, tuples) for
an optimized read/write implementation.

This can be useful outside of sequences as well, for example on newtype structs
containing byte arrays with `#[repr(transparent)]`.

💡 **Note:** as of `wincode` `0.2.0`, `pod_wrapper!` is no longer needed for types that wincode
can determine are “memcpy-safe”.

This includes:

- `u8`
- `[u8; N]`
- structs comprised of the above, and;
- annotated with `#[derive(SchemaWrite)]`or`#[derive(SchemaRead)]`, and;
- annotated with `#[repr(transparent)]`or`#[repr(C)]`.

- annotated with

Similarly, using built-in std collections like `Vec<T>` or `Box<[T]>` where `T` is one of the
above will also be automatically optimized.

You’ll really only need to reach for [ pod_wrapper!](https://docs.rs/macro.pod_wrapper.html) when dealing with foreign types for which
you cannot derive

`SchemaWrite` or `SchemaRead`. Or you’re in a controlled scenario where you
explicitly want to avoid endianness or layout checks.[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

- The type must allow any bit pattern (e.g., no `bool`s, no`char`s, etc.)
- If used on a compound type like a struct, all fields must be also be memcpy-able, its layout
must be guaranteed (via `#[repr(transparent)]`or`#[repr(C)]`), and the struct must not have any padding.
- Must not contain references or pointers (includes types like `Vec`or`Box`).- Note, you may use `pod_wrapper!`created types*inside*types like`Vec`or`Box`, e.g.,`Vec<PodT>`or`Box<[PodT]>`, but using`pod_wrapper!`on the outer type is invalid.

- Note, you may use

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

A repr-transparent newtype struct containing a byte array where you cannot derive `SchemaWrite`
or `SchemaRead`:

```
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize, Clone, Copy)]
#[repr(transparent)]
struct Address([u8; 32]);
wincode::pod_wrapper! {
    unsafe struct PodAddress(Address);
}
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize, SchemaWrite, SchemaRead)]
struct MyStruct {
    #[wincode(with = "PodAddress")]
    address: Address
}
let my_struct = MyStruct {
    address: Address(array::from_fn(|i| i as u8)),
};
let wincode_bytes = wincode::serialize(&my_struct).unwrap();
let bincode_bytes = bincode::serialize(&my_struct).unwrap();
assert_eq!(wincode_bytes, bincode_bytes);
```

# TypeMeta in wincode - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wincode/^0.5.0/enum.TypeMeta.html

## Expand description

Indicates what kind of assumptions can be made when encoding or decoding a type.

Readers and writers may use this to optimize their behavior.

## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Static)

### Static

The type has a statically known serialized size.

Specifying this variant can have significant performance benefits, as it can allow writers to prefetch larger chunks of memory such that subsequent read/write operations in those chunks can be performed at once without intermediate bounds checks.

Specifying this variant incorrectly will almost certainly result in a panic at runtime.

Take care not to specify this on variable length types, like `Vec` or `String`, as their
serialized size will vary based on their length.

#### Fields

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Dynamic)

### Dynamic

The type has a dynamic size, and no optimizations can be made.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/wincode/schema/mod.rs.html#125-133)#### pub const fn [keep_zero_copy](https://docs.rs#method.keep_zero_copy)(self, keep_zero_copy: [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)) -> Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/wincode/schema/mod.rs.html#125-133)

#### pub const fn [keep_zero_copy](https://docs.rs#method.keep_zero_copy)(self, keep_zero_copy: [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)) -> Self

Returns this [ TypeMeta](https://docs.rs/enum.TypeMeta.html) instance with

`zero_copy` masked by `keep_zero_copy`.For `TypeMeta::Static`, this preserves `size` and computes:
`zero_copy = zero_copy && keep_zero_copy`.

For `TypeMeta::Dynamic`, this is a no-op.

This method never upgrades a type to zero-copy.

- `keep_zero_copy(true)`leaves the flag unchanged.
- `keep_zero_copy(false)`clears the flag.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/wincode/schema/mod.rs.html#184-202)#### pub const fn [join_types](https://docs.rs#method.join_types)<const N: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)>(types: [Self; [N](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.array.html)]) -> Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/wincode/schema/mod.rs.html#184-202)

#### pub const fn [join_types](https://docs.rs#method.join_types)<const N: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)>(types: [Self; [N](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.array.html)]) -> Self

Combines multiple constituent [ TypeMeta](https://docs.rs/enum.TypeMeta.html) values into one aggregate.

Intended for composite types whose constituents are serialized sequentially.

Semantics:

- If any input is `Dynamic`, returns`Dynamic`.
- Otherwise returns `Static`with:- `size = sum of all constituent sizes`
- `zero_copy = logical AND of all constituent zero_copy flags`

Notes:

- This function does **not**validate layout/padding; it only combines metadata.
- For `N = 0`, the result is`TypeMeta::Static { size: 0, zero_copy: true }`.
- The caller must ensure the summed size is meaningful for the target type.

```
use wincode::TypeMeta;
let types = [
    TypeMeta::Static { size: 1, zero_copy: true },
    TypeMeta::Static { size: 2, zero_copy: true },
    TypeMeta::Dynamic,
    TypeMeta::Static { size: 3, zero_copy: true },
];
assert_eq!(TypeMeta::join_types(types), TypeMeta::Dynamic);
```
```
use wincode::TypeMeta;
let types = [
    TypeMeta::Static { size: 1, zero_copy: true },
    TypeMeta::Static { size: 2, zero_copy: true },
    TypeMeta::Static { size: 3, zero_copy: true },
];
assert_eq!(TypeMeta::join_types(types), TypeMeta::Static { size: 6, zero_copy: true });
```
```
use wincode::TypeMeta;
let types = [
    TypeMeta::Static { size: 1, zero_copy: true },
    TypeMeta::Static { size: 2, zero_copy: false },
    TypeMeta::Static { size: 3, zero_copy: true },
];
assert_eq!(TypeMeta::join_types(types), TypeMeta::Static { size: 6, zero_copy: false });
```

# Deserialize in wincode - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wincode/^0.5.0/trait.Deserialize.html

`pub trait Deserialize<'de>: `[SchemaRead](https://docs.rs/trait.SchemaRead.html)<'de, [DefaultConfig](https://docs.rs/config/type.DefaultConfig.html)> {
    // Provided methods
    fn [deserialize](https://docs.rs#method.deserialize)(src: &'de [[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)]) -> [ReadResult](https://docs.rs/error/type.ReadResult.html)<Self::[Dst](https://docs.rs/trait.SchemaRead.html#associatedtype.Dst)> { ... }

}## Expand description

Helper over [ SchemaRead](https://docs.rs/trait.SchemaRead.html) that automatically constructs a reader
and initializes a destination.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Using containers (indirect deserialization):

```
let vec: Vec<u8> = vec![1, 2, 3];
let bytes = wincode::serialize(&vec).unwrap();
type Dst = containers::Vec<u8, BincodeLen>;
let deserialized = Dst::deserialize(&bytes).unwrap();
assert_eq!(vec, deserialized);
```
Using direct deserialization (`T::Dst = T`):

```
let vec: Vec<u8> = vec![1, 2, 3];
let bytes = wincode::serialize(&vec).unwrap();
let deserialized: Vec<u8> = wincode::deserialize(&bytes).unwrap();
assert_eq!(vec, deserialized);
```

## Provided Associated Constants[§](https://docs.rs#provided-associated-consts)

Metadata about the type’s serialization.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety-1)Safety

It is always safe to leave this as the default `TypeMeta::Dynamic`. If
you set it to `TypeMeta::Static { size, zero_copy }`, you have to ensure
the following two points:

- `size`must always correspond to the number of bytes read by- `read`.
- If `zero_copy`is`true`,`Dst`’s in-memory representation must correspond exactly to the serialized form, and all byte sequences must be valid in-memory representations of`Dst`.

## Required Associated Types[§](https://docs.rs#required-associated-types)

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

#### fn [read_with_context](https://docs.rs#tymethod.read_with_context)(

) -> [ReadResult](https://docs.rs/error/type.ReadResult.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html)>

Read into `dst` from `reader` with context.

You must initialize `dst` if **and only if** you return `Ok(())`. In the
`Err(…)` case, initializing `dst` can lead to memory leaks.

It is permissible to not initialize `dst` if `dst` is an inhabited
zero-sized type.

# SchemaReadOwned in wincode - Rust

# Serialize in wincode - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wincode/^0.5.0/trait.Serialize.html

`pub trait Serialize: `[SchemaWrite](https://docs.rs/trait.SchemaWrite.html)<[DefaultConfig](https://docs.rs/config/type.DefaultConfig.html)> {
    // Provided methods
    fn [serialize](https://docs.rs#method.serialize)(src: &Self::[Src](https://docs.rs/trait.SchemaWrite.html#associatedtype.Src)) -> [WriteResult](https://docs.rs/error/type.WriteResult.html)<[Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)>> { ... }
[serialize_into](https://docs.rs#method.serialize_into)(dst: impl [Writer](https://docs.rs/io/trait.Writer.html), src: &Self::[Src](https://docs.rs/trait.SchemaWrite.html#associatedtype.Src)) -> [WriteResult](https://docs.rs/error/type.WriteResult.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html)> { ... }
[serialized_size](https://docs.rs#method.serialized_size)(src: &Self::[Src](https://docs.rs/trait.SchemaWrite.html#associatedtype.Src)) -> [WriteResult](https://docs.rs/error/type.WriteResult.html)<[u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u64.html)> { ... }
}## Expand description

Helper over [ SchemaWrite](https://docs.rs/trait.SchemaWrite.html) that automatically constructs a writer
and serializes a source.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Using containers (indirect serialization):

```
let vec: Vec<u8> = vec![1, 2, 3];
type Src = containers::Vec<u8, BincodeLen>;
let bytes = Src::serialize(&vec).unwrap();
let deserialized: Vec<u8> = wincode::deserialize(&bytes).unwrap();
assert_eq!(vec, deserialized);
```
Using direct serialization (`T::Src = T`):

```
let vec: Vec<u8> = vec![1, 2, 3];
let bytes = wincode::serialize(&vec).unwrap();
let deserialized: Vec<u8> = wincode::deserialize(&bytes).unwrap();
assert_eq!(vec, deserialized);
```

Serialize a serializable type into a `Vec` of bytes.

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

# deserialize in wincode - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wincode/^0.5.0/fn.deserialize.html

`pub fn deserialize<'de, T>(src: &'de [`[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)]) -> [ReadResult](https://docs.rs/error/type.ReadResult.html)<T>## Expand description

Deserialize a type from the given bytes.

This is a “simplified” version of [ Deserialize::deserialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserialize.html#method.deserialize) that
requires the

`T::Dst` to be `T`. In other words, a schema type
that deserializes to itself.This helper exists to match the expected signature of `serde`’s
`Deserialize`, where types that implement `Deserialize` deserialize
into themselves. This will be true of a large number of schema types,
but wont, for example, for specialized container structures.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
let vec: Vec<u8> = vec![1, 2, 3];
let bytes = wincode::serialize(&vec).unwrap();
let deserialized: Vec<u8> = wincode::deserialize(&bytes).unwrap();
assert_eq!(vec, deserialized);
```

# deserialize_exact in wincode - Rust

extra.push(0xAA);
assert!(wincode::deserialize_exact::<u64>(&extra).is_err());
```

# UninitBuilder in wincode - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wincode/^0.5.0/derive.UninitBuilder.html

```
#[derive(UninitBuilder)]
{
    // Attributes available to this derive:
    #[wincode]
}
```
**crate feature**only.

`derive`## Expand description

Include placement initialization helpers for structs.

This generates an `UninitBuilder` for the given struct, providing convenience
methods that can avoid a lot of boilerplate when implementing custom
`SchemaRead` implementations. In particular, it provides methods that
deal with projecting subfields of structs into `MaybeUninit`s. Without this,
one would have to write a litany of `&mut *(&raw mut (*dst_ptr).field).cast()` to
access MaybeUninit struct fields. It also provides initialization helpers and
drop tracking logic.

For example:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
#[derive(UninitBuilder)]
struct Message {
    payload: Vec<u8>,
    bytes: [u8; 32],
}
unsafe impl<'de, C: Config> SchemaRead<'de, C> for Message {
    type Dst = Self;
    fn read(mut reader: impl Reader<'de>, dst: &mut MaybeUninit<Self::Dst>) -> ReadResult<()> {
        let msg_builder = MessageUninitBuilder::<C>::from_maybe_uninit_mut(dst);
        // Deserializes a `Vec<u8>` into the `payload` slot of `Message` and marks the field
        // as initialized. If the subsequent `read_bytes` call fails, the `payload` field will
        // be dropped.
        msg_builder.read_payload(reader.by_ref())?;
        msg_builder.read_bytes(reader)?;
        msg_builder.finish();
    }
}
```
We cannot do this for enums, given the lack of facilities for placement initialization.

# log - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/log/^0.4.25/

## Expand description

A lightweight logging facade.

The `log` crate provides a single logging API that abstracts over the
actual logging implementation. Libraries can use the logging API provided
by this crate, and the consumer of those libraries can choose the logging
implementation that is most suitable for its use case.

If no logging implementation is selected, the facade falls back to a “noop” implementation that ignores all log messages. The overhead in this case is very small - just an integer load, comparison and jump.

A log request consists of a *target*, a *level*, and a *body*. A target is a
string which defaults to the module path of the location of the log request,
though that default may be overridden. Logger implementations typically use
the target to filter requests based on some user configuration.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

The basic use of the log crate is through the five logging macros: [ error!](https://docs.rs/macro.error.html),

[,](https://docs.rs/macro.warn.html)

`warn!`[,](https://docs.rs/macro.info.html)

`info!`[and](https://docs.rs/macro.debug.html)

`debug!`[where](https://docs.rs/macro.trace.html)

`trace!``error!` represents the highest-priority log messages
and `trace!` the lowest. The log messages are filtered by configuring
the log level to exclude messages with a lower priority.
Each of these macros accept format strings similarly to [.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/macro.println.html)

`println!`Avoid writing expressions with side-effects in log statements. They may not be evaluated.

[§](https://docs.rs#in-libraries)In libraries

Libraries should link only to the `log` crate, and use the provided
macros to log whatever information will be useful to downstream consumers.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use log::{info, warn};
pub fn shave_the_yak(yak: &mut Yak) {
    info!(target: "yak_events", "Commencing yak shaving for {yak:?}");
    loop {
        match find_a_razor() {
            Ok(razor) => {
                info!("Razor located: {razor}");
                yak.shave(razor);
                break;
            }
            Err(err) => {
                warn!("Unable to locate a razor: {err}, retrying");
            }
        }
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#in-executables)In executables

Executables should choose a logging implementation and initialize it early in the runtime of the program. Logging implementations will typically include a function to do this. Any log messages generated before the implementation is initialized will be ignored.

The executable itself may use the `log` crate to log as well.

[§](https://docs.rs#warning)Warning

The logging system may only be initialized once.

[§](https://docs.rs#structured-logging)Structured logging

If you enable the `kv` feature you can associate structured values
with your log records. If we take the example from before, we can include
some additional context besides what’s in the formatted message:

```
use log::{info, warn};
pub fn shave_the_yak(yak: &mut Yak) {
    info!(target: "yak_events", yak:serde; "Commencing yak shaving");
    loop {
        match find_a_razor() {
            Ok(razor) => {
                info!(razor; "Razor located");
                yak.shave(razor);
                break;
            }
            Err(e) => {
                warn!(e:err; "Unable to locate a razor, retrying");
            }
        }
    }
}
```
See the [ kv](https://docs.rs/kv/index.html) module documentation for more details.

[§](https://docs.rs#available-logging-implementations)Available logging implementations

In order to produce log output executables have to use a logger implementation compatible with the facade. There are many available implementations to choose from, here are some of the most popular ones:

- Simple minimal loggers:
- Complex configurable frameworks:
- Adaptors for other facilities:
- For WebAssembly binaries:
- For dynamic libraries:
- You may need to construct an FFI-safe wrapper over `log`to initialize in your libraries

- You may need to construct an FFI-safe wrapper over
- Utilities:

[§](https://docs.rs#implementing-a-logger)Implementing a Logger

Loggers implement the [ Log](https://docs.rs/trait.Log.html) trait. Here’s a very basic example that simply
logs all messages at the

[,](https://docs.rs/enum.Level.html)

`Error`[or](https://docs.rs/enum.Level.html)

`Warn`[levels to stdout:](https://docs.rs/enum.Level.html)

`Info````
use log::{Record, Level, Metadata};
struct SimpleLogger;
impl log::Log for SimpleLogger {
    fn enabled(&self, metadata: &Metadata) -> bool {
        metadata.level() <= Level::Info
    }
    fn log(&self, record: &Record) {
        if self.enabled(record.metadata()) {
            println!("{} - {}", record.level(), record.args());
        }
    }
    fn flush(&self) {}
}
```
Loggers are installed by calling the [ set_logger](https://docs.rs/fn.set_logger.html) function. The maximum
log level also needs to be adjusted via the

[function. The logging facade uses this as an optimization to improve performance of log messages at levels that are disabled. It’s important to set it, as it defaults to](https://docs.rs/fn.set_max_level.html)

`set_max_level`[, so no log messages will ever be captured! In the case of our example logger, we’ll want to set the maximum log level to](https://docs.rs/enum.LevelFilter.html)

`Off`[, since we ignore any](https://docs.rs/enum.LevelFilter.html)

`Info`[or](https://docs.rs/enum.Level.html)

`Debug`[level log messages. A logging implementation should provide a function that wraps a call to](https://docs.rs/enum.Level.html)

`Trace`[and](https://docs.rs/fn.set_logger.html)

`set_logger`[, handling initialization of the logger:](https://docs.rs/fn.set_max_level.html)

`set_max_level````
use log::{SetLoggerError, LevelFilter};
static LOGGER: SimpleLogger = SimpleLogger;
pub fn init() -> Result<(), SetLoggerError> {
    log::set_logger(&LOGGER)
        .map(|()| log::set_max_level(LevelFilter::Info))
}
```
Implementations that adjust their configurations at runtime should take care to adjust the maximum log level as well.

[§](https://docs.rs#use-with-std)Use with `std`

`set_logger` requires you to provide a `&'static Log`, which can be hard to
obtain if your logger depends on some runtime configuration. The
`set_boxed_logger` function is available with the `std` Cargo feature. It is
identical to `set_logger` except that it takes a `Box<Log>` rather than a
`&'static Log`:

```
pub fn init() -> Result<(), SetLoggerError> {
    log::set_boxed_logger(Box::new(SimpleLogger))
        .map(|()| log::set_max_level(LevelFilter::Info))
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#compile-time-filters)Compile time filters

Log levels can be statically disabled at compile time by enabling one of these Cargo features:

- `max_level_off`
- `max_level_error`
- `max_level_warn`
- `max_level_info`
- `max_level_debug`
- `max_level_trace`

Log invocations at disabled levels will be skipped and will not even be present in the
resulting binary. These features control the value of the `STATIC_MAX_LEVEL` constant. The
logging macros check this value before logging a message. By default, no levels are disabled.

It is possible to override this level for release builds only with the following features:

- `release_max_level_off`
- `release_max_level_error`
- `release_max_level_warn`
- `release_max_level_info`
- `release_max_level_debug`
- `release_max_level_trace`

Libraries should avoid using the max level features because they’re global and can’t be changed once they’re set.

For example, a crate can disable trace level logs in debug builds and trace, debug, and info level logs in release builds with the following configuration:

```
[dependencies]
log = { version = "0.4", features = ["max_level_debug", "release_max_level_warn"] }
```
[§](https://docs.rs#crate-feature-flags)Crate Feature Flags

The following crate feature flags are available in addition to the filters. They are
configured in your `Cargo.toml`.

- `std`allows use of- `std`crate instead of the default- `core`. Enables using- `std::error`and- `set_boxed_logger`functionality.
- `serde`enables support for serialization and deserialization of- `Level`and- `LevelFilter`.

```
[dependencies]
log = { version = "0.4", features = ["std", "serde"] }
```
[§](https://docs.rs#version-compatibility)Version compatibility

The 0.3 and 0.4 versions of the `log` crate are almost entirely compatible. Log messages
made using `log` 0.3 will forward transparently to a logger implementation using `log` 0.4. Log
messages made using `log` 0.4 will forward to a logger implementation using `log` 0.3, but the
module path and file name information associated with the message will unfortunately be lost.

# static_assertions - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/static_assertions/^1.1.0/

## Expand description

Assertions to ensure correct assumptions about constants, types, and more.

*All* checks provided by this crate are performed at [compile-time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compile_time). This
allows for finding errors quickly and early when it comes to ensuring
certain features or aspects of a codebase. These macros are especially
important when exposing a public API that requires types to be the same size
or implement certain traits.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

This crate is available [on crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/static_assertions) and can be used by adding the
following to your project’s [ Cargo.toml](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html):

```
[dependencies]
static_assertions = "1.1.0"
```
and this to your crate root (`main.rs` or `lib.rs`):

```
#[macro_use]
extern crate static_assertions;
```
When using [Rust 2018 edition](https://blog.rust-lang.org/2018/12/06/Rust-1.31-and-rust-2018.html#rust-2018), the following shorthand can help if
having `#[macro_use]` is undesirable.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Very thorough examples are provided in the docs for
[each individual macro](https://docs.rs#macros). Failure case examples are also documented.

[§](https://docs.rs#changes)Changes

See [ CHANGELOG.md](https://github.com/nvzqz/static-assertions-rs/blob/master/CHANGELOG.md)
for an exhaustive list of what has changed from one version to another.

[§](https://docs.rs#donate)Donate

This project is made freely available (as in free beer), but unfortunately
not all beer is free! So, if you would like to buy me a beer (or coffee or
*more*), then consider supporting my work that’s benefited your project
and thousands of others.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_cfg.html)- cfg
- Asserts that a given configuration is set.
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_eq_align.html)- eq_ - align
- Asserts that types are equal in alignment.
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_eq_size.html)- eq_ - size
- Asserts that types are equal in size.
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_eq_size_ptr.html)- eq_ - size_ - ptr
- Asserts that values pointed to are equal in size.
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_eq_size_val.html)- eq_ - size_ - val
- Asserts that values are equal in size.
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_fields.html)- fields
- Asserts that the type has the given fields.
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_impl_all.html)- impl_ - all
- Asserts that the type implements *all*of the given traits.
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_impl_any.html)- impl_ - any
- Asserts that the type implements *any*of the given traits.
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_impl_one.html)- impl_ - one
- Asserts that the type implements exactly one in a set of traits.
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_not_impl_all.html)- not_ - impl_ - all
- Asserts that the type does **not**implement*all*of the given traits.
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_not_impl_any.html)- not_ - impl_ - any
- Asserts that the type does **not**implement*any*of the given traits.
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_obj_safe.html)- obj_ - safe
- Asserts that the traits support dynamic dispatch
([object-safety](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch17-02-trait-objects.html#object-safety-is-required-for-trait-objects)).
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_trait_sub_all.html)- trait_ - sub_ - all
- Asserts that the trait is a child of all of the other traits.
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_trait_super_all.html)- trait_ - super_ - all
- Asserts that the trait is a parent of all of the other traits.
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_type_eq_all.html)- type_ - eq_ - all
- Asserts that *all*types in a list are equal to each other.
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_type_ne_all.html)- type_ - ne_ - all
- Asserts that *all*types are**not**equal to each other.
- [const_](https://docs.rs/macro.const_assert.html)- assert
- Asserts that constant expressions evaluate to `true`.
- [const_](https://docs.rs/macro.const_assert_eq.html)- assert_ - eq
- Asserts that constants are equal in value.
- [const_](https://docs.rs/macro.const_assert_ne.html)- assert_ - ne
- Asserts that constants are **not**equal in value.

# solana_address - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/solana-address/^2.2.0/

## Expand description

Address representation for Solana.

An address is a sequence of 32 bytes, often shown as a base58 encoded string (e.g. 14grJpemFaf88c8tiVb77W7TYg2W3ir6pfkKz3YjhhZ5).

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- Convenience macro to define a static `Address`value.
- [declare_](https://docs.rs/macro.declare_deprecated_id.html)- deprecated_ - id - `decode`
- Same as `declare_id`
- [declare_](https://docs.rs/macro.declare_id.html)- id - `decode`
- Convenience macro to declare a static address and functions to interact with it.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Address](https://docs.rs/struct.Address.html)
- The address of a [Solana account](https://solana.com/docs/core/accounts).
- [Address](https://docs.rs/struct.AddressHasher.html)- Hasher - `rand`and neither- `target_os=solana`nor BPF
- A faster, but less collision resistant hasher for addresses.
- [Address](https://docs.rs/struct.AddressHasherBuilder.html)- Hasher - Builder - `rand`and neither- `target_os=solana`nor BPF
- A builder for faster, but less collision resistant hasher for addresses.

# declare_id in solana_pubkey - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/solana-pubkey/^4.2.0/macro.declare_id.html

```
macro_rules! declare_id {
    ($address:expr) => { ... };
}
```
## Expand description

Convenience macro to declare a static address and functions to interact with it.

Input: a single literal base58 string representation of a program’s ID.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use std::str::FromStr;
use solana_address::{declare_id, Address};
declare_id!("My11111111111111111111111111111111111111111");
let my_id = Address::from_str("My11111111111111111111111111111111111111111").unwrap();
assert_eq!(id(), my_id);
```

# pubkey in solana_pubkey - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/solana-pubkey/^4.2.0/macro.pubkey.html

```
macro_rules! pubkey {
    ($input:literal) => { ... };
}
```
## Expand description

Convenience macro to define a static `Address` value.

Input: a single literal base58 string representation of an `Address`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use std::str::FromStr;
use solana_address::{address, Address};
static ID: Address = address!("My11111111111111111111111111111111111111111");
let my_id = Address::from_str("My11111111111111111111111111111111111111111").unwrap();
assert_eq!(ID, my_id);
```

# Pubkey in solana_pubkey - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/solana-pubkey/^4.2.0/struct.Pubkey.html

`pub struct Pubkey(/* private fields */);`## Expand description

The address of a [Solana account](https://solana.com/docs/core/accounts).

Some account addresses are [ed25519](https://ed25519.cr.yp.to/) public keys, with corresponding secret
keys that are managed off-chain. Often, though, account addresses do not
have corresponding secret keys — as with [ program derived
addresses](https://solana.com/docs/core/cpi#program-derived-addresses) — or the secret key is not relevant to the operation
of a program, and may have even been disposed of. As running Solana programs
can not safely create or manage secret keys, the full

[is not defined in](https://docs.rs/solana-sdk/latest/solana_sdk/signer/keypair/struct.Keypair.html)

`Keypair``solana-program` but in `solana-sdk`.## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/solana-address/2.6.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/solana_address/derive.rs.html#35-39)

[Source](https://docs.rs/solana-address/2.6.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/solana_address/derive.rs.html#35-39)

Derive a [program address](https://solana.com/docs/core/pda) from the given seeds, optional bump and
program id.

In general, the derivation uses an optional bump (byte) value to ensure a
valid PDA (off-curve) is generated. Even when a program stores a bump to
derive a program address, it is necessary to use the
[ Address::create_program_address](https://docs.rs/struct.Pubkey.html#method.create_program_address) to validate the derivation. In
most cases, the program has the correct seeds for the derivation, so it would
be sufficient to just perform the derivation and compare it against the
expected resulting address.

This function avoids the cost of the `create_program_address` syscall
(`1500` compute units) by directly computing the derived address
calculating the hash of the seeds, bump and program id using the
`sol_sha256` syscall.

[§](https://docs.rs#important)Important

This function differs from [ Address::create_program_address](https://docs.rs/struct.Pubkey.html#method.create_program_address) in that
it does not perform a validation to ensure that the derived address is a valid
(off-curve) program derived address. It is intended for use in cases where the
seeds, bump, and program id are known to be valid, and the caller wants to derive
the address without incurring the cost of the

`create_program_address` syscall.[Source](https://docs.rs/solana-address/2.6.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/solana_address/derive.rs.html#96-100)

[Source](https://docs.rs/solana-address/2.6.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/solana_address/derive.rs.html#96-100)

Derive a [program address](https://solana.com/docs/core/pda) from the given seeds, optional bump and
program id.

In general, the derivation uses an optional bump (byte) value to ensure a valid PDA (off-curve) is generated.

This function is intended for use in `const` contexts - i.e., the seeds and
bump are known at compile time and the program id is also a constant. It avoids
the cost of the `create_program_address` syscall (`1500` compute units) by
directly computing the derived address using the SHA-256 hash of the seeds,
bump and program id.

[§](https://docs.rs#important-1)Important

This function differs from [ Address::create_program_address](https://docs.rs/struct.Pubkey.html#method.create_program_address) in that
it does not perform a validation to ensure that the derived address is a valid
(off-curve) program derived address. It is intended for use in cases where the
seeds, bump, and program id are known to be valid, and the caller wants to derive
the address without incurring the cost of the

`create_program_address` syscall.This function is a compile-time constant version of [ Address::derive_address](https://docs.rs/struct.Pubkey.html#method.derive_address).
It has worse performance than

`derive_address`, so only use this function in
`const` contexts, where all parameters are known at compile-time.[Source](https://docs.rs/solana-address/2.6.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/solana_address/derive.rs.html#141-144)

[Source](https://docs.rs/solana-address/2.6.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/solana_address/derive.rs.html#141-144)

Attempt to derive a valid [program derived address](https://solana.com/docs/core/cpi#program-derived-addresses) (PDA) and its corresponding
bump seed.

The main difference between this method and [ Address::derive_address](https://docs.rs/struct.Pubkey.html#method.derive_address)
is that this method iterates through all possible bump seed values (starting from

`255` and decrementing) until it finds a valid (off-curve) program derived address.If a valid PDA is found, it returns the PDA and the bump seed used to derive it;
otherwise, it returns `None`.

[Source](https://docs.rs/solana-address/2.6.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/solana_address/syscalls.rs.html#277)#### pub fn [find_program_address](https://docs.rs#method.find_program_address)(
    seeds: &[&[[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)]],
    program_id: &[Address](https://docs.rs/struct.Pubkey.html),
) -> ([Address](https://docs.rs/struct.Pubkey.html), [u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html))

`target_os=solana` or BPF or crate feature `curve25519`

[Source](https://docs.rs/solana-address/2.6.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/solana_address/syscalls.rs.html#277)

#### pub fn [find_program_address](https://docs.rs#method.find_program_address)(
    seeds: &[&[[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)]],
    program_id: &[Address](https://docs.rs/struct.Pubkey.html),
) -> ([Address](https://docs.rs/struct.Pubkey.html), [u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html))

**only.**

`target_os=solana` or BPF or crate feature `curve25519`Find a valid [program derived address](https://solana.com/docs/core/cpi#program-derived-addresses) and its corresponding bump seed.

Program derived addresses (PDAs) are account keys that only the program,
`program_id`, has the authority to sign. The address is of the same form
as a Solana `Address`, except they are ensured to not be on the ed25519
curve and thus have no associated private key. When performing
cross-program invocations the program can “sign” for the key by calling
[ invoke_signed](https://docs.rs/solana-program/latest/solana_program/program/fn.invoke_signed.html) and passing the same seeds used to generate the
address, along with the calculated

*bump seed*, which this function returns as the second tuple element. The runtime will verify that the program associated with this address is the caller and thus authorized to be the signer.

The `seeds` are application-specific, and must be carefully selected to
uniquely derive accounts per application requirements. It is common to
use static strings and other addresses as seeds.

Because the program address must not lie on the ed25519 curve, there may
be seed and program id combinations that are invalid. For this reason,
an extra seed (the bump seed) is calculated that results in a
point off the curve. The bump seed must be passed as an additional seed
when calling `invoke_signed`.

The processes of finding a valid program address is by trial and error, and even though it is deterministic given a set of inputs it can take a variable amount of time to succeed across different inputs. This means that when called from an on-chain program it may incur a variable amount of the program’s compute budget. Programs that are meant to be very performant may not want to use this function because it could take a considerable amount of time. Programs that are already at risk of exceeding their compute budget should call this with care since there is a chance that the program’s budget may be occasionally and unpredictably exceeded.

As all account addresses accessed by an on-chain Solana program must be
explicitly passed to the program, it is typical for the PDAs to be
derived in off-chain client programs, avoiding the compute cost of
generating the address on-chain. The address may or may not then be
verified by re-deriving it on-chain, depending on the requirements of
the program. This verification may be performed without the overhead of
re-searching for the bump key by using the [ create_program_address](https://docs.rs/struct.Pubkey.html#method.create_program_address)
function.

**Warning**: Because of the way the seeds are hashed there is a potential
for program address collisions for the same program id.  The seeds are
hashed sequentially which means that seeds {“abcdef”}, {“abc”, “def”},
and {“ab”, “cd”, “ef”} will all result in the same program address given
the same program id. Since the chance of collision is local to a given
program id, the developer of that program must take care to choose seeds
that do not collide with each other. For seed schemes that are susceptible
to this type of hash collision, a common remedy is to insert separators
between seeds, e.g. transforming {“abc”, “def”} into {“abc”, “-”, “def”}.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

Panics in the statistically improbable event that a bump seed could not be
found. Use [ try_find_program_address](https://docs.rs/struct.Pubkey.html#method.try_find_program_address) to handle this case.

Panics if any of the following are true:

- the number of provided seeds is greater than, *or equal to*,`crate::MAX_SEEDS`
- any individual seed’s length is greater than `crate::MAX_SEED_LEN`

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

This example illustrates a simple case of creating a “vault” account which is derived from the payer account, but owned by an on-chain program. The program derived address is derived in an off-chain client program, which invokes an on-chain Solana program that uses the address to create a new account owned and controlled by the program itself.

By convention, the on-chain program will be compiled for use in two different contexts: both on-chain, to interpret a custom program instruction as a Solana transaction; and off-chain, as a library, so that clients can share the instruction data structure, constructors, and other common code.

First the on-chain Solana program:

```
// The custom instruction processed by our program. It includes the
// PDA's bump seed, which is derived by the client program. This
// definition is also imported into the off-chain client program.
// The computed address of the PDA will be passed to this program via
// the `accounts` vector of the `Instruction` type.
#[derive(BorshSerialize, BorshDeserialize, Debug)]
pub struct InstructionData {
    pub vault_bump_seed: u8,
    pub lamports: u64,
}
// The size in bytes of a vault account. The client program needs
// this information to calculate the quantity of lamports necessary
// to pay for the account's rent.
pub static VAULT_ACCOUNT_SIZE: u64 = 1024;
// The entrypoint of the on-chain program, as provided to the
// `entrypoint!` macro.
fn process_instruction(
    program_id: &Address,
    accounts: &[AccountInfo],
    instruction_data: &[u8],
) -> ProgramResult {
    let account_info_iter = &mut accounts.iter();
    let payer = next_account_info(account_info_iter)?;
    // The vault PDA, derived from the payer's address
    let vault = next_account_info(account_info_iter)?;
    let mut instruction_data = instruction_data;
    let instr = InstructionData::deserialize(&mut instruction_data)?;
    let vault_bump_seed = instr.vault_bump_seed;
    let lamports = instr.lamports;
    let vault_size = VAULT_ACCOUNT_SIZE;
    // Invoke the system program to create an account while virtually
    // signing with the vault PDA, which is owned by this caller program.
    invoke_signed(
        &create_account(
            &payer.key,
            &vault.key,
            lamports,
            vault_size,
            program_id,
        ),
        &[
            payer.clone(),
            vault.clone(),
        ],
        // A slice of seed slices, each seed slice being the set
        // of seeds used to generate one of the PDAs required by the
        // callee program, the final seed being a single-element slice
        // containing the `u8` bump seed.
        &[
            &[
                b"vault",
                payer.key.as_ref(),
                &[vault_bump_seed],
            ],
        ]
    )?;
    Ok(())
}
```
The client program:

```
fn create_vault_account(
    client: &RpcClient,
    program_id: Address,
    payer: &Keypair,
) -> Result<()> {
    // Derive the PDA from the payer account, a string representing the unique
    // purpose of the account ("vault"), and the address of our on-chain program.
    let (vault_address, vault_bump_seed) = Address::find_program_address(
        &[b"vault", payer.pubkey().as_ref()],
        &program_id
    );
    // Get the amount of lamports needed to pay for the vault's rent
    let vault_account_size = usize::try_from(VAULT_ACCOUNT_SIZE)?;
    let lamports = client.get_minimum_balance_for_rent_exemption(vault_account_size)?;
    // The on-chain program's instruction data, imported from that program's crate.
    let instr_data = InstructionData {
        vault_bump_seed,
        lamports,
    };
    // The accounts required by both our on-chain program and the system program's
    // `create_account` instruction, including the vault's address.
    let accounts = vec![
        AccountMeta::new(payer.pubkey(), true),
        AccountMeta::new(vault_address, false),
        AccountMeta::new(solana_system_interface::program::ID, false),
    ];
    // Create the instruction by serializing our instruction data via borsh
    let instruction = Instruction::new_with_borsh(
        program_id,
        &instr_data,
        accounts,
    );
    let blockhash = client.get_latest_blockhash()?;
    let transaction = Transaction::new_signed_with_payer(
        &[instruction],
        Some(&payer.pubkey()),
        &[payer],
        blockhash,
    );
    client.send_and_confirm_transaction(&transaction)?;
    Ok(())
}
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/solana-address/2.6.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/solana_address/syscalls.rs.html#300-303)`target_os=solana` or BPF or crate feature `curve25519`

[Source](https://docs.rs/solana-address/2.6.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/solana_address/syscalls.rs.html#300-303)

**only.**

`target_os=solana` or BPF or crate feature `curve25519`Find a valid [program derived address](https://solana.com/docs/core/cpi#program-derived-addresses) and its corresponding bump seed.

The only difference between this method and [ find_program_address](https://docs.rs/struct.Pubkey.html#method.find_program_address)
is that this one returns

`None` in the statistically improbable event
that a bump seed cannot be found; or if any of `find_program_address`’s
preconditions are violated.See the documentation for [ find_program_address](https://docs.rs/struct.Pubkey.html#method.find_program_address) for a full description.

[Source](https://docs.rs/solana-address/2.6.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/solana_address/syscalls.rs.html#392-395)#### pub fn [create_program_address](https://docs.rs#method.create_program_address)(
    seeds: &[&[[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)]],
    program_id: &[Address](https://docs.rs/struct.Pubkey.html),
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[Address](https://docs.rs/struct.Pubkey.html), [AddressError](https://docs.rs/enum.PubkeyError.html)>

`target_os=solana` or BPF or crate feature `curve25519`

[Source](https://docs.rs/solana-address/2.6.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/solana_address/syscalls.rs.html#392-395)

#### pub fn [create_program_address](https://docs.rs#method.create_program_address)(
    seeds: &[&[[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)]],
    program_id: &[Address](https://docs.rs/struct.Pubkey.html),
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[Address](https://docs.rs/struct.Pubkey.html), [AddressError](https://docs.rs/enum.PubkeyError.html)>

**only.**

`target_os=solana` or BPF or crate feature `curve25519`Create a valid [program derived address](https://solana.com/docs/core/cpi#program-derived-addresses) without searching for a bump seed.

Because this function does not create a bump seed, it may unpredictably return an error for any given set of seeds and is not generally suitable for creating program derived addresses.

However, it can be used for efficiently verifying that a set of seeds plus
bump seed generated by [ find_program_address](https://docs.rs/struct.Pubkey.html#method.find_program_address) derives a particular
address as expected. See the example for details.

See the documentation for [ find_program_address](https://docs.rs/struct.Pubkey.html#method.find_program_address) for a full description
of program derived addresses and bump seeds.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-1)Examples

Creating a program derived address involves iteratively searching for a
bump seed for which the derived [ Address](https://docs.rs/struct.Pubkey.html) does not lie on the ed25519
curve. This search process is generally performed off-chain, with the

[function, after which the client passes the bump seed to the program as instruction data.](https://docs.rs/struct.Pubkey.html#method.find_program_address)

`find_program_address`Depending on the application requirements, a program may wish to verify that the set of seeds, plus the bump seed, do correctly generate an expected address.

The verification is performed by appending to the other seeds one
additional seed slice that contains the single `u8` bump seed, calling
`create_program_address`, checking that the return value is `Ok`, and
that the returned `Address` has the expected value.

```
let (expected_pda, bump_seed) = Address::find_program_address(&[b"vault"], &program_id);
let actual_pda = Address::create_program_address(&[b"vault", &[bump_seed]], &program_id)?;
assert_eq!(expected_pda, actual_pda);
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/solana-address/2.6.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/solana_address/lib.rs.html#223)

#### pub fn [is_on_curve](https://docs.rs#method.is_on_curve)(&self) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

**crate features**only.

`curve25519` or `syscalls`Checks whether the given address lies on the Ed25519 curve.

On-curve addresses correspond to valid Ed25519 public keys (and therefore can have associated private keys). Off-curve addresses are typically used for program-derived addresses (PDAs).

# PubkeyHasher in solana_pubkey - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/solana-pubkey/^4.2.0/struct.PubkeyHasher.html

`pub struct PubkeyHasher { /* private fields */ }`**crate feature**only.

`rand` and non-`target_os=solana`## Expand description

A faster, but less collision resistant hasher for addresses.

Specialized hasher that uses a random 8 bytes subslice of the address as the hash value. Should not be used when collisions might be used to mount DOS attacks.

Using this results in about 4x faster lookups in a typical hashmap.

# PubkeyHasherBuilder in solana_pubkey - Rust

`pub struct PubkeyHasherBuilder { /* private fields */ }`**crate feature**only.

`rand` and non-`target_os=solana`## Expand description

A builder for faster, but less collision resistant hasher for addresses.

Initializes `AddressHasher` instances that use an 8-byte
slice of the address as the hash value. Should not be used when
collisions might be used to mount DOS attacks.

Using this results in about 4x faster lookups in a typical hashmap.

[§](https://docs.rs#method.default)

#### fn [default](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/default/trait.Default.html#tymethod.default)() -> [AddressHasherBuilder](https://docs.rs/struct.PubkeyHasherBuilder.html)

Default construct the AddressHasherBuilder.

The position of the slice is determined initially
through random draw and then by incrementing a thread-local
This way each hashmap can be expected to use a slightly different
slice. This is essentially the same mechanism as what is used by
`RandomState`

[27](#27)pub fn verify_nonce_account(
[30](#30)    account: &AccountSharedData,
[31](#31)    recent_blockhash: &Hash, ) -> Option<Data> {
[33](#33)    (account.owner() == &system_program::id())
[34](#34)        .then(|| {
[35](#35)            #[cfg(feature = "wincode")]
[36](#36)            let versions = wincode::deserialize::<Versions>(account.data());
[37](#37)            #[cfg(not(feature = "wincode"))]
[38](#38)            let versions = StateMut::<Versions>::state(account);
[39](#39)            versions
[40](#40)                .ok()?
[41](#41)                .verify_recent_blockhash(recent_blockhash)
[42](#42)                .cloned()
[43](#43)        })
[44](#44)        .flatten()
[45](#45)}
[46](#46)
[47](#47)pub fn lamports_per_signature_of(account: &AccountSharedData) -> Option<u64> {
[48](#48)    match StateMut::<Versions>::state(account).ok()?.state() {
[49](#49)        State::Initialized(data) => Some(data.fee_calculator.lamports_per_signature),
[50](#50)        State::Uninitialized => None,
[51](#51)    }

[58](#58)}
[59](#59)
[60](#60)pub fn get_system_account_kind(account: &AccountSharedData) -> Option<SystemAccountKind> {
[61](#61)    if system_program::check_id(account.owner()) {
[62](#62)        if account.data().is_empty() {
[63](#63)            Some(SystemAccountKind::System)
[64](#64)        } else if account.data().len() == State::size() {
[65](#65)            let nonce_versions: Versions = account.state().ok()?;
[66](#66)            match nonce_versions.state() {
[67](#67)                State::Uninitialized => None,
[68](#68)                State::Initialized(_) => Some(SystemAccountKind::Nonce),
[69](#69)            }
[70](#70)        } else {
[71](#71)            None
[72](#72)        }
[73](#73)    } else {
[74](#74)        None
[75](#75)    }

[137](#137)        );
[138](#138)        let durable_nonce = DurableNonce::from_blockhash(durable_nonce.as_hash());
[139](#139)        assert_ne!(data.durable_nonce, durable_nonce);
[140](#140)        let data = Data {
[141](#141)            durable_nonce,
[142](#142)            ..data
[143](#143)        };
[144](#144)        let versions = Versions::Current(Box::new(State::Initialized(data.clone())));
[145](#145)        let account = new_nonce_account(versions);
[146](#146)        assert_eq!(verify_nonce_account(&account, &blockhash), None);
[147](#147)        assert_eq!(verify_nonce_account(&account, &Hash::default()), None);
[148](#148)        assert_eq!(
[149](#149)            verify_nonce_account(&account, &data.blockhash()),
[150](#150)            Some(data.clone())
[151](#151)        );
[152](#152)        assert_eq!(
[153](#153)            verify_nonce_account(&account, durable_nonce.as_hash()),
[154](#154)            Some(data)
[155](#155)        );
[156](#156)    }
[157](#157)

# clap - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/clap

## Expand description

Command Line Argument Parser for Rust

Quick Links:

- Derive [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_derive/_tutorial/index.html)and[reference](https://docs.rs/_derive/index.html)
- Builder [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_tutorial/index.html)and[reference](https://docs.rs/struct.Command.html)
- [Cookbook](https://docs.rs/_cookbook/index.html)
- [CLI Concepts](https://docs.rs/_concepts/index.html)
- [FAQ](https://docs.rs/_faq/index.html)
- [Discussions](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/discussions)
- [CHANGELOG](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/blob/v4.6.1/CHANGELOG.md)(includes major version migration guides)

[§](https://docs.rs#aspirations)Aspirations

- Out of the box, users get a polished CLI experience
- Including common argument behavior, help generation, suggested fixes for users, colored output, [shell completions](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/tree/master/clap_complete), etc

- Including common argument behavior, help generation, suggested fixes for users, colored output,
- Flexible enough to port your existing CLI interface
- However, we won’t necessarily streamline support for each use case

- Reasonable parse performance
- Resilient maintainership, including
- Willing to break compatibility rather than batching up breaking changes in large releases
- Leverage feature flags to keep to one active branch
- Being under [WG-CLI](https://github.com/rust-cli/team/)to increase the bus factor

- We follow semver and will wait about 6-9 months between major breaking changes
- We will support the last two minor Rust releases (MSRV, currently 1.74)

While these aspirations can be at odds with fast build times and low binary
size, we will still strive to keep these reasonable for the flexibility you
get.  Check out the
[argparse-benchmarks](https://github.com/rust-cli/argparse-benchmarks-rs) for
CLI parsers optimized for other use cases.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

Run

`$ cargo add clap --features derive`*(See also  feature flag reference)*

Then define your CLI in `main.rs`:

```
use clap::Parser;
/// Simple program to greet a person
#[derive(Parser, Debug)]
#[command(version, about, long_about = None)]
struct Args {
    /// Name of the person to greet
    #[arg(short, long)]
    name: String,
    /// Number of times to greet
    #[arg(short, long, default_value_t = 1)]
    count: u8,
}
fn main() {
    let args = Args::parse();
    for _ in 0..args.count {
        println!("Hello {}!", args.name);
    }
}
```
And try it out:

```
$ demo --help
A simple to use, efficient, and full-featured Command Line Argument Parser
Usage: demo[EXE] [OPTIONS] --name <NAME>
Options:
  -n, --name <NAME>    Name of the person to greet
  -c, --count <COUNT>  Number of times to greet [default: 1]
  -h, --help           Print help
  -V, --version        Print version
$ demo --name Me
Hello Me!
```
*(version number and  .exe extension on windows replaced by placeholders)*

See also the derive [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_derive/_tutorial/index.html) and [reference](https://docs.rs/_derive/index.html)

[§](https://docs.rs#related-projects)Related Projects

Augment clap:

- [wild](https://crates.io/crates/wild)for supporting wildcards (- `*`) on Windows like you do Linux
- [argfile](https://crates.io/crates/argfile)for loading additional arguments from a file (aka response files)
- [shadow-rs](https://crates.io/crates/shadow-rs)for generating- `Command::long_version`
- [clap_mangen](https://crates.io/crates/clap_mangen)for generating man page source (roff)
- [clap_complete](https://crates.io/crates/clap_complete)for shell completion support
- [clap-i18n-richformatter](https://crates.io/crates/clap-i18n-richformatter)for i18n support with- `clap::error::RichFormatter`

CLI Helpers

- [clio](https://crates.io/crates/clio)for reading/writing to files specified as arguments
- [clap-verbosity-flag](https://crates.io/crates/clap-verbosity-flag)
- [clap-cargo](https://crates.io/crates/clap-cargo)
- [colorchoice-clap](https://crates.io/crates/colorchoice-clap)

Testing

- `trycmd`
- `snapbox`
- `assert_cmd`- `assert_fs`

Documentation:

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [arg](https://docs.rs/macro.arg.html)
- Create an `Arg`
- [command](https://docs.rs/macro.command.html)- `cargo`
- Allows you to build the `Command`instance from your Cargo.toml at compile time.
- [crate_](https://docs.rs/macro.crate_authors.html)- authors - `cargo`
- Allows you to pull the authors for the command from your Cargo.toml at
compile time in the form:
`"author1 lastname <author1@example.com>:author2 lastname <author2@example.com>"`
- [crate_](https://docs.rs/macro.crate_description.html)- description - `cargo`
- Allows you to pull the description from your Cargo.toml at compile time.
- [crate_](https://docs.rs/macro.crate_name.html)- name - `cargo`
- Allows you to pull the name from your Cargo.toml at compile time.
- [crate_](https://docs.rs/macro.crate_version.html)- version - `cargo`
- Allows you to pull the version from your Cargo.toml at compile time as
`MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH_PKGVERSION_PRE`
- [value_](https://docs.rs/macro.value_parser.html)- parser
- Select a `ValueParser`

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Arg](https://docs.rs/struct.Arg.html)
- The abstract representation of a command line argument. Used to set all the options and relationships that define a valid argument for the program.
- [ArgGroup](https://docs.rs/struct.ArgGroup.html)
- Specifies a logical group of [arguments](https://docs.rs/struct.Arg.html)
- [ArgMatches](https://docs.rs/struct.ArgMatches.html)
- Container for parse results.
- [Command](https://docs.rs/struct.Command.html)
- Build a command-line interface.
- [Id](https://docs.rs/struct.Id.html)
- `Arg`- `ArgGroup`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [ArgAction](https://docs.rs/enum.ArgAction.html)
- Behavior of arguments when they are encountered while parsing
- [Color](https://docs.rs/enum.ColorChoice.html)- Choice
- Represents the color preferences for program output
- [Value](https://docs.rs/enum.ValueHint.html)- Hint
- Provide shell with hint on how to complete an argument.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Args](https://docs.rs/trait.Args.html)
- Parse a set of arguments into a user-defined container.
- [Command](https://docs.rs/trait.CommandFactory.html)- Factory
- Create a `Command`
- [From](https://docs.rs/trait.FromArgMatches.html)- ArgMatches
- Converts an instance of `ArgMatches`
- [Parser](https://docs.rs/trait.Parser.html)
- Parse command-line arguments into `Self`.
- [Subcommand](https://docs.rs/trait.Subcommand.html)
- Parse a sub-command into a user-defined enum.
- [Value](https://docs.rs/trait.ValueEnum.html)- Enum
- Parse arguments into enums.

- Converts an instance of `ArgMatches`

- [Subcommand](https://docs.rs/trait.Subcommand.html)
- Parse a sub-command into a user-defined enum.

- Parse arguments into enums.
